title: HTML document structure and semantic page regions
description: Learn how a complete HTML document is organized, why metadata belongs in the head, how the browser treats the body, and how semantic elements communicate the purpose of page regions.
learningOutcomes: Explain the purpose of the doctype, html, head, and body parts of an HTML document.
Distinguish document metadata from content intended to appear in the page.
Choose between header, nav, main, section, article, and footer based on meaning rather than appearance.
Build a small, correctly structured About Me page and inspect it with browser DevTools.
Embed third-party or user-authored content with an accessible name and a least-privilege sandbox boundary.

blocks.text: Why document structure matters

HTML is a markup language: its elements describe the structure and meaning of content. It is not the visual design system—that is mainly the job of CSS—and it is not the behavior layer—that is usually handled by JavaScript. A well-structured document gives the browser a predictable input, helps assistive technology expose meaningful navigation, and makes the code easier for other developers to understand.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.text: Treat an HTML file as a structured document with two broad areas: the head describes the document to browsers and other systems; the body contains the document's page content. Semantic elements inside the body explain what each region is for. CSS can change how these regions look without changing their underlying meaning.
The four main parts of an HTML document

The following is a complete minimal document. Modern browsers can repair many omissions, so a page may appear to work even when its source is incomplete. Do not use that error recovery as a substitute for writing a deliberate document structure.

steps.title: <!doctype html>
steps.explanation: The doctype tells the browser to use standards mode for the document. In modern HTML it is the simple declaration shown here; it is not a normal HTML element and it does not wrap page content.

steps.title: <html lang="en">
steps.explanation: The html element is the root of the document. The lang attribute identifies the main language of the page and helps assistive technologies pronounce content appropriately. Use a valid language tag for the actual document language.

steps.title: <head>
steps.explanation: The head contains machine-readable document metadata such as character encoding, viewport behavior, title, description, links to stylesheets, and other resources. The metadata is not ordinary visible page content.

steps.title: <body>
steps.explanation: The body contains the page's content: headings, paragraphs, images, links, forms, and semantic page regions. In a rendered page, most content the learner interacts with comes from here.

blocks.text: What the metadata actually does

items: `meta charset="utf-8"` declares the character encoding. UTF-8 is the expected default for modern web documents and supports a broad range of scripts.
`meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1` gives mobile browsers a viewport width aligned with the device width and an initial scale suitable for responsive layouts.
`title` supplies the document title shown in browser tabs and used in other browser and platform contexts. It is different from the visible `h1` heading.
`meta name="description"` provides a short page description that search engines may use as a result snippet; it does not guarantee the exact snippet that will be displayed.
`lang` belongs on the root `html` element and should match the primary language of the page.

blocks.title: Do not confuse head and header
blocks.text: `<head>` is document metadata. `<header>` is a semantic element inside page content, usually introducing a page or a section. Similar names do not mean they have the same role.
Semantic regions: describe purpose, not appearance

Semantic HTML uses elements that express the role of their content. Do not choose an element because it looks like a certain visual layout; use CSS for appearance and choose HTML according to meaning. These elements can improve navigation for assistive technologies and make a codebase easier to maintain, but semantics do not automatically make an entire page accessible.

items: `header`: introductory content or navigation aids for the page or a section. A page can contain more than one header when sections need their own introductory area.
`nav`: a major group of navigation links, such as a primary menu or table of contents. Not every group of links needs to be wrapped in nav.
`main`: the dominant content of the page. Normally use one visible main element for the page's primary content.
`section`: a thematic grouping of related content, generally with its own heading. It is not just a generic replacement for every div.
`article`: a self-contained composition that could make sense independently, such as a post, news item, or forum entry.
`footer`: information about the nearest page or section, such as related links, authorship or copyright.

items: The header introduces the site and groups the primary navigation.
The main element contains the content that is central to this particular page.
Each section groups one topic and has a heading that tells the reader what to expect.

blocks.title: section vs div
blocks.text: Use section when the content forms a meaningful thematic section, usually with a heading. Use div when you need a generic container for styling or scripting and the grouping itself has no special semantic meaning. Using semantic elements everywhere is not better if the chosen meaning is inaccurate.

blocks.prompt: Where should the document title that appears in a browser tab normally be declared?

options.text: In a title element inside head
options.feedback: The title element belongs in the document head and supplies the document title.

options.text: In the first h1 inside body
options.feedback: An h1 is a visible content heading. It may resemble the title, but it serves a different purpose.
Header is part of the page content and has no special role as the browser-tab title.
Footer content describes a page or section ending; it does not define the browser-tab title.

blocks.explanation: Document metadata belongs in head. Visible headings belong in body, even when the title and main heading use similar wording.

blocks.prompt: A page contains a self-contained blog post that can be shared or reused independently. Which element is the strongest semantic fit for the post itself?

options.feedback: Article is intended for a self-contained composition that can make sense independently.
Nav identifies a major navigation region, not a content post.
Main marks the page's dominant content region, not the semantic type of an individual post inside it.
Head contains document metadata and is not a visible content container for the post.

blocks.explanation: Choose semantic elements based on the role and independence of their content, not on its styling or position.

blocks.text: Choose text elements for meaning, not default appearance

Use `strong` for importance and `em` for emphasis; `b` and `i` can draw attention or mark a different voice without adding the same importance/emphasis meaning. `mark` highlights content relevant to the current context. `code` marks a code fragment. `br` is a line break within content such as an address or verse, not a spacing tool; `hr` marks a thematic break. Keep heading levels in a logical content hierarchy instead of selecting them for their default font size.

steps.title: Give important or emphasized words their meaning
steps.explanation: `strong` conveys importance, `em` conveys emphasis, and `mark` calls out contextually relevant text. They may have visual styles, but the semantic meaning is the point.

steps.title: Distinguish semantic emphasis from visual voice
steps.explanation: `b` and `i` can indicate attention or an alternate voice without making the same claim as `strong` and `em`. Choose an element based on the content and intent.

steps.title: Use line and thematic breaks appropriately
steps.explanation: `br` creates a line break within content where the break is meaningful. `hr` indicates a thematic break. Neither should be used as a substitute for CSS layout and spacing.

steps.title: Mark up inline code
steps.explanation: The `code` element marks a code fragment; `pre` is commonly used when a preformatted block needs to preserve whitespace. Neither runs JavaScript by itself.

blocks.prompt: A sentence describes a critical requirement. Which element most clearly marks the text as important, beyond making it bold?

options.feedback: Strong marks content as having strong importance; browsers commonly render it bold, but its purpose is semantic.
B draws attention without adding the same strong-importance meaning.
A styled span changes appearance but does not communicate the same native meaning.
Br creates a line break and does not mark a passage as important.

blocks.explanation: Choose text markup according to the role of the content; CSS controls appearance independently.

blocks.text: Links, metadata, and global attributes

An anchor's `href` determines its destination; use link text that explains where it goes instead of repeating vague labels such as “click here.” When a link opens a new tab, explain that behavior when it matters and use `rel="noopener"` to prevent access through `window.opener`; add `noreferrer` when suppressing the referrer is also intended. In `head`, a description can be used as a search-result snippet but does not guarantee the snippet, while Open Graph metadata supports social-sharing previews. Global attributes have different jobs: `id` is a unique document identifier, `class` groups elements for styling, `data-*` stores application-specific data, and `lang` identifies the language of a content subtree. Use `hidden` only when content should be hidden from presentation and interaction, and avoid positive `tabindex` values that disrupt natural focus order.

steps.title: Make the destination understandable
steps.explanation: The href provides the destination and the text names the link purpose. `target="_blank"` opens a new browsing context; `rel="noopener"` blocks access to the opener. `noreferrer` is an additional choice when referrer information should not be sent.

steps.title: Separate document and sharing metadata
steps.explanation: The description meta element may be used as a result snippet, but search engines choose their displayed text. Open Graph properties provide metadata used by sharing platforms; they are not visible body content.

steps.title: Use global attributes for their intended role
steps.explanation: An id must be unique in the document; data attributes can expose application-specific values to scripts. Prefer native controls and natural tab order instead of using attributes as substitutes for semantics.

items: `id`: identifies one element in the document; keep it unique so labels, fragments and scripts resolve predictably.
`class`: groups elements for CSS and other class-based behavior; classes can be reused.
`data-*`: exposes custom data values on an element for scripts without inventing nonstandard attributes.
`hidden`: indicates that the element is not currently relevant for display; do not use it just to visually move content off-screen for accessibility.
`lang`: identifies the language of an element's text when it differs from the surrounding document language.
`tabindex="0"` can place a custom focusable element in normal sequential focus order; `tabindex="-1"` permits programmatic focus without adding it to that order. Avoid positive values.
`title` may provide advisory information but is not a replacement for a visible label, clear link text or instructions.

blocks.text: Use tables for relationships between data

A data table expresses row/column relationships; it is not a layout grid. Give the table a concise caption, mark column headers with `th scope="col"`, and row headers with `th scope="row"`. Keep each cell's relationship understandable when navigating by keyboard or screen reader. A table with complex multi-level headers may need explicit `id`/`headers` associations; do not add them to a simple table without a reason. For narrow screens, allow a deliberate scroll/reflow strategy instead of hiding columns or forcing tiny text.

blocks.text: Media needs a semantic and accessible alternative

An informative image needs concise alternative text that conveys its purpose in context; a decorative image should use an empty alt so assistive technology can skip it. Use figure/figcaption when a caption belongs to the media. Audio/video controls provide browser playback controls, but they do not create captions or transcripts for you. Video with meaningful speech or sound needs synchronized captions; provide a transcript when useful, and avoid autoplaying media that can surprise or distract users.

steps.title: Describe the meaningful image, not its filename
steps.explanation: The alt communicates what the sketch shows. The caption adds context that is visible to everyone; if an image is purely decorative, use alt="" instead.

steps.title: Give the user playback control and a lightweight initial load
steps.explanation: controls exposes native playback controls. preload="metadata" hints that the browser can fetch basic media information without eagerly downloading the full video; it is a hint, not a guarantee.

steps.title: Provide captions as a separate text resource
steps.explanation: The track references a WebVTT captions file with a language label. Controls alone are not captions; verify timing, speaker identification and meaningful non-speech audio in the actual track.

blocks.prompt: A diagram conveys information that is not already explained in nearby text. What should its img alternative text do?

options.text: Describe the diagram's relevant information concisely in context
options.feedback: Alternative text should communicate the image's purpose or essential content, not repeat its filename.

options.text: Repeat the filename, including the .png extension
options.feedback: A filename rarely communicates the image's meaning to a reader.

options.text: Always begin with the words 'image of'
options.feedback: Assistive technology already identifies an image; use the available text for its useful purpose.
Empty alt is appropriate for decorative images, not informative content.

blocks.explanation: Choose alt based on the image's role on the page; nearby text can change what information needs to be conveyed.

blocks.text: Embed content with an explicit trust boundary

An iframe embeds a separate browsing context. Give it a descriptive `title` so assistive-technology users can identify the frame, and treat the URL as a trust decision: third-party content can still display misleading UI even when cross-origin rules limit script access to the parent. The `sandbox` attribute starts with restrictions; add only the tokens the embedded feature needs. `allow-scripts` permits the frame's scripts. `allow-same-origin` preserves its origin instead of assigning an opaque origin. If same-origin untrusted content receives both tokens, it can access the embedding document and remove the sandbox, defeating the boundary. For user-provided or untrusted content, prefer a separate origin and the smallest permissions. Offer a normal link as a fallback when embedding fails.

blocks.code: Open the report

steps.title: Name the embedded browsing context
steps.explanation: A descriptive title distinguishes the frame from the parent page in assistive-technology navigation. The external origin is a deliberate trust boundary, not proof that the content is harmless.

steps.title: Begin with sandbox restrictions
steps.explanation: An empty sandbox value applies the restrictions by default. Add a specific token only after confirming the provider needs that capability; do not copy a permission list as a magic preset.

steps.title: Keep a usable fallback
steps.explanation: The ordinary link gives users a path if the embed is blocked, unavailable, or unsuitable on their device. Lazy loading is useful for offscreen content, not a security control.

blocks.prompt: An untrusted same-origin iframe must run scripts. Why is adding both `allow-scripts` and `allow-same-origin` to its sandbox dangerous?

options.text: The iframe will always be blocked by the browser.
options.feedback: The tokens grant capabilities; they do not automatically block the frame. The risk comes from combining them for same-origin content.

options.text: The frame can access its same-origin parent and remove the sandbox, defeating the restrictions.
options.feedback: With both capabilities and the same origin, the embedded document can reach the parent DOM and remove its own iframe's sandbox attribute.

options.text: The frame becomes unable to load images.
options.feedback: Image loading is not the central consequence of this permission combination.

options.text: The frame's title becomes hidden from screen readers.
options.feedback: The title provides an accessible name. It is independent of these sandbox capabilities.

blocks.explanation: Sandbox tokens are individual privilege grants. Keep untrusted content on a separate origin and allow only what its job requires.

items: A document doctype, root html element, head metadata and body content have distinct jobs.
The title in head and the visible h1 in body are not interchangeable.
Semantic elements communicate purpose; CSS controls appearance.
Use main for primary page content, section for thematic groups, article for self-contained compositions, nav for major navigation, and header/footer for introductory or concluding information.
A browser rendering a page successfully does not prove that its structure is intentional or accessible.

blocks.text: Deep dive: semantic structure, landmarks, and accessible names

HTML semantics describe the role of content, not its visual appearance. A `nav` element communicates a navigation landmark; `main` identifies the page's primary content; `article` represents a self-contained composition. Semantic elements help assistive technology and make a page's structure easier to navigate. Use the element whose meaning fits the content instead of choosing a generic `div` only because it looks easier to style.

steps.title: Declare the language and document metadata
steps.explanation: The document declaration selects standards mode; the language helps assistive technology choose pronunciation; charset and viewport metadata are practical basics for a modern page.

steps.title: Use a real link and a named navigation landmark
steps.explanation: A link provides native keyboard behavior and a destination. The label distinguishes the primary navigation landmark when a page has multiple nav regions.

steps.title: Represent the page hierarchy with semantics
steps.explanation: main, article, heading, and footer each communicate a role. Do not add a landmark merely to obtain styling, and keep a clear primary heading for the page content.

items: Keep heading levels meaningful and in a logical hierarchy; don't choose an h2 because its default font size looks right.
Write link text that makes sense out of context. Repeated links all named 'Click here' give screen-reader users little information.
Choose alternative text based on the image's purpose: informative images need a concise equivalent; decorative images should not create noisy redundant descriptions.
Use native HTML controls before building custom widgets. Buttons, links, headings, forms and tables already provide behavior and semantics that custom div-based controls would need to recreate.
HTML parsing can repair malformed markup in ways different from the source author's intent; use valid nesting and inspect the resulting DOM in DevTools when rendered structure surprises you.

blocks.prompt: Which is the best reason to use a semantic `nav` element instead of a styled `div` for primary site navigation?

options.text: It automatically makes every link secure
options.feedback: HTML semantics do not enforce network security or authorization.

options.text: It communicates a navigation landmark and uses native link semantics for navigation
options.feedback: Assistive technology can identify navigation regions, while anchor elements preserve native navigation behavior.

options.text: It guarantees the page has perfect SEO
options.feedback: Semantic markup helps communicate structure but cannot guarantee search ranking or overall page quality.

options.text: It always renders faster than a div
options.feedback: The main reason here is meaning and accessibility, not a reliable performance difference.

blocks.explanation: Prefer elements for their semantics and behavior, then style them with CSS.
